# Eigenvalues, Invariant Subspaces, and Their Sensitivity


The eigenvalue problem $\bA\bv = \lambda\bv$ identifies the invariant one-dimensional subspaces of a linear operator. Along an eigenvector $\bv$, the action of the matrix $\bA$ reduces to scalar scaling by $\lambda$. Eigenvalues govern the asymptotic stability of dynamical systems, the resonant frequencies of mechanical and electrical systems, the convergence rates of iterative solvers, and the dominant invariant coordinates in spectral graph theory and data science.


The characteristic equation $\det(\bA-\lambda\bI)=0$ is useful for definitions and small examples, but forming its coefficients is not a sound numerical algorithm. Forming the coefficients discards the matrix structure and replaces one problem by a polynomial root problem that may be far more sensitive. Practical methods work with the matrix directly and use orthogonal or unitary transformations whenever possible.


We first define eigenvalues and invariant subspaces and relate them to changes of basis. We then prove the Schur and spectral theorems, characterize the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix by Rayleigh quotients, and use that characterization to bound how far eigenvalues move when the matrix is perturbed. Algorithms for computing eigenvalues are the subject of the referenced section.


## Invariant Directions and Change of Basis


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
Let $\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}$. A nonzero vector $\bv \in \fC^n$ is an eigenvector of $\bA$ associated with eigenvalue $\lambda \in \fC$ if
$$
\begin{align}
\bA\bv = \lambda\bv.
\end{align}
$$
The set of eigenvalues is the spectrum $\sigma(\bA)$. When eigenvalues are listed as $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_n$, repetitions are included according to algebraic multiplicity.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Invariant Subspace
A subspace $S\subseteq\fC^n$ is **invariant** under $\bA$ if $\bA\bx\in S$ whenever $\bx\in S$. An eigenvector spans a one-dimensional invariant subspace. Higher-dimensional invariant subspaces remain meaningful even when no basis of eigenvectors exists.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Example
Three two-dimensional examples show what the definition can and cannot promise.

1. A diagonal matrix scales the coordinate axes, leaving both axes invariant.

1. The shear $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has only one independent eigenvector. Repeated application keeps sliding vectors in the same direction, so a repeated eigenvalue need not supply a full eigenbasis.

1. A nontrivial planar rotation has no real invariant line, but it has complex eigenvectors. The complex eigenvalues encode the rotation as multiplication by a complex phase.

:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Similarity and a Change of Basis
Matrices $\bA$ and $\bB$ are **similar** if
$$
\begin{align}
\bB=\bS^{-1}\bA\bS
\end{align}
$$
for some nonsingular $\bS$. They represent the same linear map in different bases: the columns of $\bS$ are the new basis vectors written in the old coordinates.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Similarity Preserves Eigenvalues
If $\bB=\bS^{-1}\bA\bS$, then $\bA$ and $\bB$ have the same eigenvalues. More precisely, $\bA\bv=\lambda\bv$ if and only if
$$
\begin{align}
\bB(\bS^{-1}\bv)=\lambda(\bS^{-1}\bv).
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
Multiplying $\bA\bv=\lambda\bv$ by $\bS^{-1}$ and inserting $\bS\bS^{-1}=\bI$ gives
$$
\begin{align}
(\bS^{-1}\bA\bS)(\bS^{-1}\bv)
    =\lambda(\bS^{-1}\bv).
\end{align}
$$
The reverse implication follows by multiplying by $\bS$.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Diagonalization Means an Eigenvector Basis
A matrix $\bA\in\fC^{n\times n}$ is similar to a diagonal matrix if and only if it has a basis of eigenvectors. If $\bS=(\bv_1\ \cdots\ \bv_n)$ contains such a basis, then
$$
\begin{align}
\bA\bS=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda},
    \qquad
    \bA=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bS^{-1}.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
If the columns of $\bS$ are eigenvectors, the $j$th columns of $\bA\bS$ and $\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ are both $\lambda_j\bv_j$, which proves the factorization. Conversely, if $\bA=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bS^{-1}$, then $\bA\bS=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$, so each column of the nonsingular matrix $\bS$ is an eigenvector.
:::


## Multiplicity and Schur Form


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Algebraic and Geometric Multiplicity
Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $\bA$.

1. The algebraic multiplicity $\mu_a(\lambda)$ is the multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a root of $\det(\bA - z\bI) = 0$.

1. The geometric multiplicity $\mu_g(\lambda) = \dim \mathcal{N}(\bA - \lambda\bI)$ is the dimension of the corresponding eigenspace.

Every eigenvalue satisfies $1 \leq \mu_g(\lambda) \leq \mu_a(\lambda)$. When $\mu_g(\lambda) < \mu_a(\lambda)$ for any eigenvalue, $\bA$ is defective and does not possess a complete basis of eigenvectors.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Schur Triangularization Decomposition
Every square matrix $\bA \in \fC^{n \times n}$ is unitarily similar to an upper triangular matrix:
$$
\begin{align}
\bA = \bQ\bT\bQ^*,
\end{align}
$$
where $\bQ \in \fC^{n \times n}$ is unitary ($\bQ^*\bQ = \bI$) and $\bT \in \fC^{n \times n}$ is upper triangular. The diagonal entries of $\bT$ are the eigenvalues of $\bA$.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
We proceed by induction on the matrix dimension $n$. For $n = 1$, the statement holds trivially with $\bQ = [1]$ and $\bT = \bA$.

Assume the theorem holds for all square matrices of order $n - 1$. By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, the characteristic polynomial $\det(\bA - z\bI) = 0$ possesses at least one complex root $\lambda_1$. Let $\bv_1 \in \fC^n$ be an eigenvector associated with $\lambda_1$, normalized so that $\|\bv_1\|_2 = 1$. Using the Gram--Schmidt process or Householder reflectors, construct an orthonormal basis for $\fC^n$ whose first column is $\bv_1$, forming a unitary matrix $\bU_1 = [\bv_1, \bW] \in \fC^{n \times n}$ with $\bW \in \fC^{n \times (n-1)}$.

Applying this unitary similarity transformation to $\bA$ gives
$$
\begin{align}
\bU_1^* \bA \bU_1
    =
    \begin{pmatrix} \bv_1^* \\ \bW^* \end{pmatrix} \bA \begin{pmatrix} \bv_1 & \bW \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix} \bv_1^* \bA \bv_1 & \bv_1^* \bA \bW \\ \bW^* \bA \bv_1 & \bW^* \bA \bW \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
$$
Because $\bA\bv_1 = \lambda_1 \bv_1$, the leading entry is $\bv_1^*(\lambda_1\bv_1) = \lambda_1 \|\bv_1\|_2^2 = \lambda_1$. The lower-left block is $\bW^*(\lambda_1\bv_1) = \lambda_1(\bW^*\bv_1) = \bzero$, because the columns of $\bW$ are orthogonal to $\bv_1$. Thus
$$
\begin{align}
\bU_1^* \bA \bU_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bw^* \\ \bzero & \bA_1 \end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
$$
where $\bA_1 = \bW^* \bA \bW \in \fC^{(n-1) \times (n-1)}$ and $\bw^* = \bv_1^* \bA \bW$.

By the induction hypothesis, there exists a unitary matrix $\bQ_1 \in \fC^{(n-1) \times (n-1)}$ such that $\bQ_1^* \bA_1 \bQ_1 = \bT_1$ is upper triangular. Define the $n \times n$ block-diagonal unitary matrix
$$
\begin{align}
\bV = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \bzero \\ \bzero & \bQ_1 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
$$
Setting $\bQ = \bU_1 \bV$, which is unitary as the product of unitary matrices, we obtain
$$
\begin{align}
\bQ^* \bA \bQ
    =
    \bV^* (\bU_1^* \bA \bU_1) \bV
    =
    \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \bzero \\ \bzero & \bQ_1^* \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bw^* \\ \bzero & \bA_1 \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \bzero \\ \bzero & \bQ_1 \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bw^* \bQ_1 \\ \bzero & \bQ_1^* \bA_1 \bQ_1 \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bw^* \bQ_1 \\ \bzero & \bT_1 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
$$
Because $\bT_1$ is upper triangular, the entire block matrix $\bT = \bQ^*\bA\bQ$ is upper triangular. The diagonal entries of $\bT$ are $\lambda_1$ and the eigenvalues of $\bA_1$, which collectively form the eigenvalues of $\bA$.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Spectral Theorem for Real Symmetric Matrices
If $\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}$ is real symmetric ($\bA = \bA^T$), then all eigenvalues of $\bA$ are real, and $\bA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable:
$$
\begin{align}
\bA = \bQ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bQ^T = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \bq_i \bq_i^T,
\end{align}
$$
where $\bQ \in \fR^{n \times n}$ is real orthogonal ($\bQ^T\bQ = \bI$) and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, ..., \lambda_n)$ is real diagonal.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
First, let $\lambda \in \fC$ and $\bv \in \fC^n \setminus \{\bzero\}$ satisfy $\bA\bv = \lambda\bv$. Taking the inner product with $\bv$,
$$
\begin{align}
\bv^*\bA\bv = \bv^*(\lambda\bv) = \lambda\|\bv\|_2^2.
\end{align}
$$
Taking the conjugate transpose of this scalar and using $\bA = \bA^T = \bA^*$,
$$
\begin{align}
\bv^*\bA\bv = (\bv^*\bA\bv)^* = (\lambda\|\bv\|_2^2)^* = \bar{\lambda}\|\bv\|_2^2.
\end{align}
$$
Subtracting these two scalar expressions gives
$$
\begin{align}
(\lambda - \bar{\lambda})\|\bv\|_2^2 = 0.
\end{align}
$$
Because $\bv \neq \bzero$, $\|\bv\|_2^2 > 0$, forcing $\lambda = \bar{\lambda} \in \fR$. Thus all eigenvalues are real.

Because $\lambda_1 \in \fR$ and $\bA$ is real, writing $\bv = \bx + i\by$ gives $\bA\bx = \lambda_1\bx$ and $\bA\by = \lambda_1\by$. At least one of $\bx,\by$ is nonzero, yielding a real unit eigenvector $\bq_1$. Extend $\bq_1$ to an orthogonal matrix $\bQ_1 = [\bq_1, \bW] \in \fR^{n \times n}$ with $\bW \in \fR^{n \times (n-1)}$. Because $\bA\bq_1 = \lambda_1\bq_1$ and $\bW^T\bq_1 = \bzero$:
$$
\begin{align}
\bQ_1^T\bA\bQ_1
    =
    \begin{pmatrix} \bq_1^T \\ \bW^T \end{pmatrix} \bA \begin{pmatrix} \bq_1 & \bW \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix} \bq_1^T\bA\bq_1 & \bq_1^T\bA\bW \\ \bW^T\bA\bq_1 & \bW^T\bA\bW \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & (\bW^T\bA\bq_1)^T \\ \bzero & \bA_1 \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bzero^T \\ \bzero & \bA_1 \end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
$$
where $\bA_1 = \bW^T\bA\bW \in \fR^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}$ is symmetric. By induction on dimension, there exists an orthogonal $\bQ_2 \in \fR^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}$ such that $\bQ_2^T\bA_1\bQ_2 = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_2, ..., \lambda_n)$. The matrix
$$
\begin{align}
\bQ = \bQ_1 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \bzero \\ \bzero & \bQ_2 \end{pmatrix}
\end{align}
$$
is orthogonal and satisfies $\bQ^T\bA\bQ = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}$, so $\bA = \bQ\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bQ^T$.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Courant--Fischer Minimax Theorem
Let $\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}$ be real symmetric with eigenvalues ordered as $\lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq ... \leq \lambda_n$. Then for each $k \in \{1, ..., n\}$,
$$
\begin{align}
\lambda_k = \min_{\dim(S) = k} \max_{\bx \in S,\, \bx \neq \bzero} \frac{\bx^T \bA \bx}{\bx^T \bx}
    =
    \max_{\dim(S) = n - k + 1} \min_{\bx \in S,\, \bx \neq \bzero} \frac{\bx^T \bA \bx}{\bx^T \bx}.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
Let $\bq_1, ..., \bq_n$ be an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $\bA$ with $\bA\bq_i = \lambda_i \bq_i$. For any nonzero $\bx = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \bq_i$, the Rayleigh quotient satisfies
$$
\begin{align}
R(\bx) = \frac{\bx^T\bA\bx}{\bx^T\bx} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2}.
\end{align}
$$
Define the subspace $V_k = \operatorname{span}\{\bq_1, ..., \bq_k\}$, which has dimension $k$. For any nonzero $\bx \in V_k$, $c_i = 0$ for all $i > k$, so
$$
\begin{align}
R(\bx) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^k c_i^2} \leq \lambda_k \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k c_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^k c_i^2} = \lambda_k.
\end{align}
$$
Because $\bq_k \in V_k$ achieves $R(\bq_k) = \lambda_k$, we have $\max_{\bx \in V_k,\, \bx \neq \bzero} R(\bx) = \lambda_k$.

Now let $S$ be any arbitrary subspace of $\fR^n$ with $\dim(S) = k$. Define $W_{k-1} = \operatorname{span}\{\bq_k, ..., \bq_n\}$, which has dimension $n - k + 1$. By the dimension formula,
$$
\begin{align}
\dim(S \cap W_{k-1}) = \dim(S) + \dim(W_{k-1}) - \dim(S + W_{k-1}) \geq k + (n - k + 1) - n = 1.
\end{align}
$$
Therefore, there exists a nonzero vector $\by \in S \cap W_{k-1}$. Because $\by \in W_{k-1}$, its expansion $\by = \sum_{i=k}^n d_i \bq_i$ contains only modes $i \geq k$, so
$$
\begin{align}
R(\by) = \frac{\sum_{i=k}^n \lambda_i d_i^2}{\sum_{i=k}^n d_i^2} \geq \lambda_k \frac{\sum_{i=k}^n d_i^2}{\sum_{i=k}^n d_i^2} = \lambda_k.
\end{align}
$$
Because $\by \in S$, the maximum over $S$ satisfies $\max_{\bx \in S,\, \bx \neq \bzero} R(\bx) \geq R(\by) \geq \lambda_k$. Taking the minimum over all $k$-dimensional subspaces $S$ proves the first equality. The dual maximum-minimum characterization follows similarly by replacing $\bA$ with $-\bA$.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Cauchy Interlacing Theorem
Let $\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, and let $\bB\in\fR^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}$ be a principal submatrix. If
$$
\begin{align}
\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n,
    \qquad
    \mu_1\leq\cdots\leq\mu_{n-1}
\end{align}
$$
are the eigenvalues of $\bA$ and $\bB$, respectively, then
$$
\begin{align}
\lambda_k\leq\mu_k\leq\lambda_{k+1},
    \qquad k=1,...,n-1.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
After a simultaneous permutation of rows and columns, we may assume that $\bB$ is obtained by deleting the last row and column. Identify $\fR^{n-1}$ with the coordinate hyperplane
$$
\begin{align}
H=\{\bx\in\fR^n:x_n=0\}.
\end{align}
$$
For every nonzero $\bx\in H$, the Rayleigh quotients of $\bA$ and $\bB$ agree.

Apply the first Courant--Fischer characterization from the referenced result. The minimization defining $\mu_k$ ranges only over $k$-dimensional subspaces of $H$, whereas the minimization defining $\lambda_k$ ranges over all $k$-dimensional subspaces of $\fR^n$. Restricting the admissible set cannot decrease the minimum, so $\lambda_k\leq\mu_k$.

For the other inequality, use the dual characterization. Since $\dim(H)=n-1$,
$$
\begin{align}
\mu_k
    &=\max_{\substack{S\subset H\\ \dim(S)=n-k}}
      \min_{\bx\in S,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R_{\bA}(\bx)
    \leq\max_{\substack{S\subset\fR^n\\ \dim(S)=n-k}}
      \min_{\bx\in S,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R_{\bA}(\bx)
      =\lambda_{k+1}.
\end{align}
$$
Together the two bounds give the interlacing inequalities.
:::


## Sensitivity of Eigenvalues


Every eigenvalue algorithm computes the eigenvalues of a matrix that differs from $\bA$ by rounding errors, and every iterative eigensolver stops with an approximate eigenpair whose residual is small but nonzero. We therefore need to know how far eigenvalues move when the matrix is perturbed. For symmetric matrices the answer follows from the referenced result, and eigenvalues move no farther than the norm of the perturbation. For a general diagonalizable matrix the answer also depends on the condition number of the eigenvector basis.


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Weyl's Perturbation Theorem
Let $\bA$ and $\bE$ be real symmetric $n\times n$ matrices. Let $\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of $\bA$ and $\mu_1\leq\cdots\leq\mu_n$ the eigenvalues of $\bA+\bE$. Then
$$
\begin{align}
|\mu_k-\lambda_k|\leq\|\bE\|_2,\qquad k=1,...,n.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
For every nonzero $\bx$, the Rayleigh quotients of the two matrices satisfy
$$
\begin{align}
\frac{\bx^T(\bA+\bE)\bx}{\bx^T\bx}=\frac{\bx^T\bA\bx}{\bx^T\bx}+\frac{\bx^T\bE\bx}{\bx^T\bx},
    \qquad
    \frac{|\bx^T\bE\bx|}{\bx^T\bx}\leq\frac{\|\bx\|_2\|\bE\bx\|_2}{\|\bx\|_2^2}\leq\|\bE\|_2,
\end{align}
$$
where the second relation uses Cauchy--Schwarz and the definition of the induced norm. The Rayleigh quotient of $\bA+\bE$ therefore lies within $\|\bE\|_2$ of that of $\bA$ for every $\bx$. Taking the maximum over a $k$-dimensional subspace and then the minimum over all such subspaces preserves this relation, so the first characterization in the referenced result gives $\lambda_k-\|\bE\|_2\leq\mu_k\leq\lambda_k+\|\bE\|_2$.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Corollary: Residual Bounds for Symmetric Matrices
Let $\bA$ be real symmetric, let $\bx$ be a unit vector, let $\theta$ be real, and let $\br=\bA\bx-\theta\bx$.

1. Some eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $\bA$ satisfies $|\lambda-\theta|\leq\|\br\|_2$.

1. Suppose $\theta=\bx^T\bA\bx$, let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $\bA$ nearest to $\theta$, and let $\delta>0$ be the distance from $\theta$ to the remaining eigenvalues. Then
        $$
    \begin{align}
    |\lambda-\theta|\leq\frac{\|\br\|_2^2}{\delta}.
    \end{align}
    $$

:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
Expand $\bx=\sum_ic_i\bq_i$ in an orthonormal eigenvector basis, so that $\sum_ic_i^2=1$ and $\br=\sum_i(\lambda_i-\theta)c_i\bq_i$. Then
$$
\begin{align}
\|\br\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^n(\lambda_i-\theta)^2c_i^2\geq\min_i(\lambda_i-\theta)^2,
\end{align}
$$
which proves the first claim.

For the second claim, the Rayleigh quotient condition is $\sum_i(\lambda_i-\theta)c_i^2=0$. Suppose $\lambda\leq\theta$, since the case $\lambda\geq\theta$ follows by applying the argument to $-\bA$. Let $\beta=\theta+\delta$. An eigenvalue $\lambda_i\neq\lambda$ cannot lie in $(\lambda,\theta]$, because it would then be closer to $\theta$ than $\lambda$. Such an eigenvalue also cannot lie in $(\theta,\beta)$, by the definition of $\delta$. Hence every such eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda_i<\lambda$ or $\lambda_i\geq\beta$, and in both cases $(\lambda_i-\lambda)(\lambda_i-\beta)\geq0$. The product vanishes when $\lambda_i=\lambda$. Writing $\lambda_i-\lambda=(\lambda_i-\theta)+(\theta-\lambda)$ and $\lambda_i-\beta=(\lambda_i-\theta)-\delta$ and expanding gives
$$
\begin{align}
0\leq\sum_{i=1}^n(\lambda_i-\lambda)(\lambda_i-\beta)c_i^2
    =\|\br\|_2^2+(\theta-\lambda-\delta)\sum_{i=1}^n(\lambda_i-\theta)c_i^2-(\theta-\lambda)\delta
    =\|\br\|_2^2-(\theta-\lambda)\delta.
\end{align}
$$
Therefore $(\theta-\lambda)\delta\leq\|\br\|_2^2$.
:::


The first bound states that a small residual locates an eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix to within the residual norm. The second bound shows that the Rayleigh quotient is much more accurate than its residual when the eigenvalue is well separated from the rest of the spectrum. An eigenvector residual of $10^{-4}$ and a gap of order one, for example, give an eigenvalue error of order $10^{-8}$.


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Bauer--Fike Theorem
Let $\bA=\bX\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bX^{-1}$ be diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_n$, and let $\bE$ be any $n\times n$ matrix. Every eigenvalue $\mu$ of $\bA+\bE$ satisfies
$$
\begin{align}
\min_{1\leq i\leq n}|\lambda_i-\mu|\leq\kappa_2(\bX)\|\bE\|_2,
\end{align}
$$
where $\kappa_2(\bX)=\|\bX\|_2\|\bX^{-1}\|_2$ is computed in the Euclidean norm on $\fC^n$.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
If $\mu$ is an eigenvalue of $\bA$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}-\mu\bI$ is nonsingular. Because $\bA+\bE-\mu\bI$ is singular, so is
$$
\begin{align}
\bX^{-1}(\bA+\bE-\mu\bI)\bX
    =(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}-\mu\bI)\big(\bI+(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}-\mu\bI)^{-1}\bX^{-1}\bE\bX\big).
\end{align}
$$
The second factor is singular, so the referenced result, whose proof applies without change on $\fC^n$, shows that $\|(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}-\mu\bI)^{-1}\bX^{-1}\bE\bX\|_2\geq1$. The norm of the diagonal matrix $(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}-\mu\bI)^{-1}$ is $1/\min_i|\lambda_i-\mu|$. Submultiplicativity therefore gives
$$
\begin{align}
1\leq\frac{\|\bX^{-1}\|_2\|\bE\|_2\|\bX\|_2}{\min_i|\lambda_i-\mu|},
\end{align}
$$
which is the stated bound.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Corollary: Residual Bound for Diagonalizable Matrices
Let $\bA=\bX\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bX^{-1}$, let $\bx$ be a unit vector, let $\theta\in\fC$, and let $\br=\bA\bx-\theta\bx$. Then some eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $\bA$ satisfies $|\lambda-\theta|\leq\kappa_2(\bX)\|\br\|_2$.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
The matrix $\bE=-\br\bx^*$ satisfies $(\bA+\bE)\bx=\bA\bx-\br=\theta\bx$, so $\theta$ is an eigenvalue of $\bA+\bE$. Since $\|\bE\|_2=\|\br\|_2\|\bx\|_2=\|\br\|_2$, the referenced result gives the bound.
:::


For a symmetric matrix, the referenced result provides an orthogonal $\bX$ with $\kappa_2(\bX)=1$, and the referenced result reduces to the first part of the referenced result. For a nonnormal matrix, $\kappa_2(\bX)$ can be large, and a small residual then locates an eigenvalue only loosely. Near a defective matrix the eigenvalues can move much farther than the perturbation, as the following example shows.


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Example
**(Eigenvalues of a nearly defective matrix)**
The matrix
$$
\begin{align}
\bA_\varepsilon=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ \varepsilon&0\end{pmatrix}
\end{align}
$$
differs from the defective matrix $\bA_0$ by a perturbation of norm $\varepsilon$, but its eigenvalues are $\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon}$. For $\varepsilon=10^{-10}$, a perturbation at the level of $10^{-10}$ moves the double eigenvalue zero by $10^{-5}$. The eigenvectors $(1,\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon})^T$ of $\bA_\varepsilon$ become parallel as $\varepsilon\to0$, so $\kappa_2(\bX)$ grows without bound, in agreement with the referenced result.
:::
## Exercises


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise

1. **Derive.**  **(Rayleigh quotient stationary points)**  For a real symmetric matrix $\bA$, define the Rayleigh quotient $R(\bx) = \frac{\bx^T\bA\bx}{\bx^T\bx}$ on $\fR^n \setminus \{\bzero\}$.

    1. Compute the gradient $\nabla R(\bx)$ directly.

    1. Prove that $\nabla R(\bx) = \bzero$ if and only if $\bx$ is an eigenvector of $\bA$.

    1. Restrict the Hessian $\nabla^2R(\bq_i)$ to directions orthogonal to $\bq_i$. Show that its eigenvalues on this tangent space are $\frac{2}{\|\bq_i\|_2^2}(\lambda_j-\lambda_i)$ for $j\neq i$. Explain why the radial direction has zero curvature, and conclude that the smallest and largest eigenvalues are the global extrema of $R$.

1. **Derive.**  **(Similarity is a coordinate change)**  Choose a nonorthogonal basis of $\fR^2$, form its basis matrix $\bS$, and compute $\bS^{-1}\bA\bS$ for a simple diagonal matrix $\bA$. Verify directly that eigenvalues are preserved although lengths and angles generally are not.

1. **Explore.**  **(A defective shear)**  For $\bA=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, find the algebraic and geometric multiplicities of the eigenvalue. Compute $\bA^k$ and explain how its growth is invisible if one records only the eigenvalue $1$.

1. **Compute.**  **(Cauchy interlacing on a concrete matrix)**  For
        $$
    \begin{align}
    \bA=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&2&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix},
    \end{align}
    $$
        compute the eigenvalues of $\bA$ and of the leading $2\times2$ principal submatrix. Verify each inequality in the referenced result. Repeat after deleting the middle row and column.

:::
